data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single dominant cross-city modulator is building geometry through its effect on wind speed: denser, taller building arrays reduce wind speed, trapping both anthropogenic and stored thermal mass heat, so cities with greater built density develop larger nocturnal UHI.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal UHI magnitude shows weak correlation with wind-speed reduction across cities, wind sheltering cannot be the dominant modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the largest nocturnal UHI occurs in cities with high wind speed, the mechanism is contradicted","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If calm-condition measurements show that wind speed is already negligible in both city and countryside, wind-speed reduction cannot explain the cross-city difference","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the heat retained by wind sheltering is small relative to the radiative (SVF) trapping effect, wind speed is not the single best modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban materials with high heat capacity and thermal mass store daytime solar energy and release sensible heat after sunset. Anthropogenic emissions add further heat. Dense building geometry reduces wind speed by increasing surface roughness and creating sheltered street canyons, so this combined heat is not ventilated away efficiently. The reduced wind speed slows the nocturnal cooling rate of the urban air, amplifying the nighttime temperature gap. Cities with stronger wind-speed reduction (larger building height-to-spacing ratio, greater built density) retain more heat and develop larger nocturnal UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
